transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-04 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Lucas Moreno (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Maya Lin (VP Eng, Cernova), Ravi Patel (ML Lead), Ethan Cole (Infra)

Summary: Weekly POC check-in. Main focus: bench delta vs their incumbent provider (BaselineCloudAI). Discussed recent run results, where Redwood improved median latency after routing and batching changes but still sees p99 delta and throughput plateau under long-run 120 RPS. Agreed to run longer soak and share configs.

[00:00] Lucas: all right everyone, thanks for joining. quick check, audio ok?
[00:07] Maya: yep. can hear you.
[00:09] Lucas: cool. so agenda, quick readout of the bench that ran overnight, then priya will walk tuning changes, and ravi you can add any infra notes, and we end with next steps.
[00:20] Priya: hi team. i ran three passes: cold-start baseline, warmed-kv, and quantized with dynamic batching. i can pull up the slides but i pasted the key numbers in the shared doc.
[00:32] Ravi: saw those, thanks. my infra notes are at the bottom — we limited the incumbent to their 8-gpu pool to match your dedicated slot.
[00:40] Lucas: ok, quick numbers. median latency p50: Redwood 28ms vs incumbent 45ms — so big win on medians. p95: Redwood 210ms vs incumbent 200ms — slightly worse. p99: Redwood 980ms vs incumbent 640ms — gap persists. throughput steady-state at 120 rps per model instance, Redwood plateaued earlier.
[01:05] Maya: interesting — median is great but p99 is concerning, that’s our user-facing tail. what might cause the 99th spike?
[01:12] Priya: a few likely culprits: kv-cache cold misses during some sequences, occasional larger prompt batches that force kernel fallback, and quantization jitter on certain attention patterns. we saw these correlate with longer sequences in the test set.
[01:28] Ethan: on infra side we saw some cuda context resets aligning with the p99 windows, esp around 50–55 minutes into the soak. could be memory pressure on the node - not all of it model-related.
[01:41] Lucas: good catch. priya, you mentioned routing — what did you change?
[01:45] Priya: two things: we introduced a preference for low-latency slots for the first token and then allow batching for subsequent tokens — hybrid routing — and we adjusted the batching horizon down from 30ms to 12ms for the critical route. that dropped median a lot but increases jitter for long seqs.
[02:05] Ravi: did that impact cost? more slots or lower utilization?
[02:08] Lucas: marginally; unit-cost went up by about 7% on that route but the customer saw medians improve, which matters for perceived snappiness.
[02:18] Maya: can we reproduce the p99 deterministically? like is it always tied to particular prompt shapes?
[02:22] Priya: we flagged a pattern — prompts with embedded code blocks and 1.2–1.5x token counts pushed kernel paths into larger matmul patterns that our quantized kernels handle less gracefully.
[02:36] Ravi: adding to that, the incumbent also uses a sticky routing that keeps long sequences on larger instances; we tried to keep parity but their steady-state slot count behaved slightly differently.
[02:49] Lucas: okay — so next experiments: long (12h) soak with a weighted mix of short and long sequences, enable deeper KV warmup, and run quantize-vs-fp32 on the same soak to compare tail behavior.
[02:59] Maya: sounds good. timeline?
[03:01] Lucas: we’ll deliver tuned config by friday — priya will send the quant table and a small script that reproduces the worst-case prompts.
[03:08] Priya: yes. also we’ll add a kernel trace sample for the p99 window so you can see exact fallback steps.
[03:14] Ethan: can you also include the node-level memory/oom logs? that will help us separate infra from model behavior.
[03:20] Priya: sure.
[03:21] Lucas: cost conversation — we showed a 12% unit-cost improvement vs incumbent on the warmed path, but if we bias for low-latency slots cost moves up. maya, what’s your tolerance vs cost?
[03:33] Maya: our product metric is 95th latency under 250ms for interactive flows, and total inference stack cost needs to be below current vendor by 5% at scale. so there's a sweet spot — we prefer p95 SLAs over p50 wins.
[03:47] Lucas: heard. we can optimize for p95 and run a variant that prioritizes tail reduction.
[03:51] Priya: quick note on caching: enabling prefix KV-cache aggressively moved many sessions out of the 99th tail because repeat prompts reused keys. hit-rate went from 23% to 68% after 15 minutes of simulated traffic; that correlated with p95 improvements.
[04:10] Ravi: the hit-rate jump is promising. how does it impact throughput?
[04:13] Priya: hit-rate up means fewer heavy matmuls, so throughput capacity rises ~18% in those windows. but warming takes time; we need a soak to see steady-state.
[04:23] Maya: ok — about the security asks, ethan, we need SSO + SAML details and encryption-at-rest notes.
[04:29] Ethan: yes, and KMS integration doc for our on-prem HSM.
[04:32] Lucas: we’ll email SOC2 and the KMS whitepaper — lucas to follow up.
[04:37] [05:00] (brief crosstalk, kids in background)
[05:15] Priya: one more thing on routing fallbacks — we configured automatic fallback to the incumbent for 503s during the last run; it worked but cost-tracking is messy. we need a clearer fallback cost accounting.
[05:29] Ravi: can we toggle fallback off for the soak run to measure pure Redwood behavior?
[05:33] Lucas: yes, we can run with fallback disabled. that will give clean numbers, though riskier for availability.
[05:39] Maya: we can accept that for a controlled 12-hour run as long as the alerting is in place.
[05:46] Priya: ok we’ll do one run with fallback off and one with fallback on to compare both latency and user-visible failures.
[05:54] Lucas: excellent. budget question — if we need dedicated continuous slots for a week to replicate production patterns, what does that look like?
[06:01] Priya: approximate snapshot: for their peak traffic estimates, a 10-slot dedicated pool for a week is roughly equivalent to X compute hours — lucas will attach exact numbers to the pricing doc.
[06:12] Maya: send that — procurement will need an estimate to sign off.
[06:15] Lucas: will do.
[06:17] [06:20] (silence while someone shares screen)
[06:25] Priya: walking through the trace now — you can see the p99 blips aligning with kernel fallback to slower attention kernel at 00:47 in the trace.
[06:35] Ravi: yep. can we instrument the runtime to emit a small metric when that fallback occurs?
[06:38] Priya: yes, lightweight event can be emitted per request, we’ll add it.
[06:42] Ethan: that will help correlate with node-level metrics.
[06:45] Maya: ok, last question — for on-prem/private deployment options: if we move to private, does the same runtime behavior hold? any differences in quant kernels?
[06:55] Priya: behavior is the same if the hardware matches; some kernel optimizations require driver stack versions we’ll list. quantized kernels are portable but need the same CUDA/cuDNN combos. we’ll include a compatibility matrix.
[07:08] Lucas: final recap — deliver tuned config, quant table, kernel traces, SOC2/KMS docs, and book a 30-min exec sync. run two 12-hour soaks (fallback off/on) and share logs.
[07:22] Maya: that covers it. thanks everyone.
[07:26] Lucas: thanks, we’ll follow up in email.
[07:30] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-attribution and filler. timestamps approximate; we sampled every ~30–90s to show flow.
